head: Safety First: How REALTORS® Can Plan, Protect and Prevail

contentHtml:
Although September is REALTOR® Safety Month, it’s always the right time to keep safety top of mind. The nature of real estate means agents often work alone, meet new clients in unfamiliar places and handle unpredictable situations. Staying alert and prepared isn’t just good practice during one month of the year—it’s a year-round commitment to protecting yourself, your business and the clients who trust you.

Every year, REALTORS® face risks in their line of work—some minor, others life-altering. The same freedom and flexibility that make real estate exciting can also make it unpredictable. Yet with the right plan, that unpredictability doesn’t have to mean danger.

Because in real estate, safety isn’t luck—it’s preparation. And preparation begins with awareness—understanding your surroundings, your clients and your instincts before every showing and interaction.

Awareness: The Foundation of Safety

Real estate professionals often work alone, in unfamiliar neighborhoods and with clients they’ve only met online. According to the National Association of REALTORS® Safety Report, more than 30% of agents say they’ve felt unsafe during a showing or open house.

This isn’t about fear—it’s about foresight. Awareness is your first defense. Before every appointment, ask yourself:

  • Do I know who I’m meeting?
  • Does anyone else know where I’ll be?
  • Have I thought through what could go wrong?

Awareness turns potential threats into managed situations.

Vetting Clients: Your First Line of Defense

Always verify a potential client’s identity. Ask to see photo identification before meeting in person—preferably at your office or through a secure verification system. Many brokerages have built-in protocols for this.

If you’re an independent agent, explain that identity verification is company policy for everyone’s safety. Serious buyers will understand. Never meet new clients at a property first. Always meet them in a public place—your office or a coffee shop—to gauge their demeanor and intent.

The Buddy System: Digital and Human

Even if you work solo, you should never be alone. Establish a system for sharing your schedule with a trusted colleague, assistant or family member. Before heading out, send them:

  • The client’s name and phone number
  • The property address
  • Expected arrival and departure times

Use safety apps such as Forewarn, Bsafe or SentriKey that allow others to track your location in real time. You can also create a discreet “safe word” for emergencies—something casual like “Can you send me the blue folder?”—to signal distress without drawing attention.

Controlling the Environment

Arrive early to check the property. Note exits, lighting and cell reception. If there’s poor signal, communicate that in your listing description or showing notes—it could be vital information for your colleagues later. Keep your vehicle parked where you can’t be blocked in, and always keep your keys accessible. During the showing, direct clients to walk in front of you rather than leading them. Stay near exits and maintain enough distance to react quickly if needed. And, never enter attics, crawl spaces or garages—places where you could become trapped or isolated.

For open houses, never host alone. Bring another agent, lender or assistant to help manage foot traffic and serve as a visible deterrent to unsafe behavior.

Trusting Your Instincts and Having an Exit Plan

Your instincts are one of your best safety tools. If something feels wrong, listen to that inner voice. Leave immediately or use a prepared excuse such as:

  • “I just realized I have another appointment.”
  • “Let’s reschedule after I confirm a few details.”
  • “My colleague will be joining us shortly.”

Once outside, get to a safe location and contact your team. Having a rehearsed exit plan ensures that you can leave any situation quickly, without hesitation or explanation.

Protecting Your Digital Presence

Safety doesn’t stop at the front door—it starts online. Be mindful of what you share on social media. Avoid real-time updates such as “On my way to show this home!” which can reveal your location. Do not overshare personal details about your home, family or daily routines. Keep personal and professional accounts separate, and use your business contact information for all client communications.

Scammers and criminals often collect pieces of public data to impersonate or track agents. Keep privacy settings strict and information minimal.

Safety as Team Culture

If you’re part of a brokerage, make safety part of the company’s culture. Hold regular training sessions or role-play scenarios to rehearse responses to difficult situations. Display emergency numbers and safety resources in visible office locations. Encourage team members to report suspicious behavior without judgment. Shared awareness is community protection.

After-Hours and Vacant Property Protocol

After-hours appointments and vacant homes require extra caution. Schedule showings during daylight when possible. If an evening appointment is unavoidable, confirm lighting and notify someone of your plans. Announce your arrival clearly: “REALTOR® here for a showing!” Check for signs of forced entry or unexpected activity. If something feels off, leave immediately and report it.

Mindset Matters

Safety begins with a clear mind and a healthy body. Fatigue, stress and overwork dull judgment. Build habits that promote alertness—proper rest, hydration and work-life balance. The better you feel, the sharper your awareness will be.

Safety isn’t a one-time checklist—it’s a mindset that grows with every showing, every client and every decision you make. By staying alert, prepared and confident, you protect not only yourself but also the trust your clients place in you. A REALTOR®’s greatest asset isn’t just knowledge of the market—it’s the ability to return home safely at the end of each day, ready to serve again tomorrow.

head: Building Strength Through Our Pillars: Advocacy, Education and Networking
excerpt: At SABOR, everything we do is grounded in three key pillars — Advocacy, Education and Networking. These pillars form the foundation of how we serve our members and strengthen the real estate profession across San Antonio and the surrounding
contentHtml:
At SABOR, everything we do is grounded in three key pillars — Advocacy, Education and Networking. These pillars form the foundation of how we serve our members and strengthen the real estate profession across San Antonio and the surrounding communities. As we move into the close of the year and look ahead to 2026, each of these pillars continues to evolve and make an impact in meaningful ways.

Advocacy: Supporting Our Communities and Our Industry

Advocacy remains at the heart of SABOR’s mission, protecting property rights, promoting fair housing and ensuring REALTORS® have a strong voice at every level of government. This year, SABOR has proudly taken a stance in support of Propositions A and B in Bexar County. These measures represent an important step toward responsible growth and investment in our region, aligning with our commitment to fostering a thriving housing market and sustainable communities.

Our Government Affairs team and REALTOR® members have been active in engaging local leaders and informing voters about the real-world impact these propositions will have on homeowners, renters and businesses alike. Whether it’s city zoning, infrastructure or affordability initiatives, SABOR continues to be a trusted advocate, ensuring that the interests of REALTORS® and their clients are represented with clarity and strength.

Advocacy is not just about legislation; it’s about leadership. Every time our members speak up for their clients, participate in voter education or build relationships with policymakers, they are contributing to a stronger, more resilient real estate community.

Education: Evolving to Meet Members’ Needs

The REALTOR® Academy has long been a cornerstone of professional development for SABOR members. As the industry shifts and technology advances, our Academy is evolving too. The team is currently working on a revamp of class offerings for 2026, with the goal of delivering education that is more meaningful, relevant and accessible than ever before.

This reimagining of our course catalog goes beyond meeting continuing education requirements. It’s about equipping REALTORS® with the knowledge and tools they need to thrive in a competitive marketplace. From in-depth courses on emerging market trends to hands-on sessions that build practical skills, SABOR is committed to helping members grow in ways that matter most to them.

Listening to our members has been central to this process. The Academy team has gathered feedback, assessed industry needs and begun shaping new programming that will ensure every SABOR member can find value in their educational experience. It’s about lifelong learning, professional excellence and the pride that comes with being part of a forward-thinking organization.

Networking: Connecting REALTORS® and Building Community

SABOR’s calendar is full of opportunities for members to connect, collaborate and celebrate. From the high-energy IMPACT 2025 event to the western-inspired Purple Party, our networking events have showcased the power of bringing REALTORS® together to share ideas, celebrate achievements and strengthen relationships.

And the year isn’t over yet! We’re gearing up for the SABOR Icon Awards, an evening dedicated to recognizing REALTORS® who go above and beyond in their service to clients, their communities and the profession. It’s more than an awards ceremony; it’s a chance to highlight the difference our members make every day and to remind ourselves why this work matters.

These gatherings embody the spirit of our organization — where professionalism meets camaraderie, and where every handshake, conversation and shared experience contributes to the greater good of our REALTOR® community.

As SABOR continues to build on these three pillars, our focus remains the same: empowering our members to succeed, advocating for the future of real estate and nurturing a network of professionals who support one another and their communities. Together, through Advocacy, Education and Networking, we’re not just shaping the future of real estate; we’re strengthening the foundation of our shared success.

head: Celebrating A Season of Connection and Growth
excerpt: The Women’s Council of REALTORS® San Antonio Network has had an incredible fall season filled with connection, celebration, and momentum as we continue to build relationships and grow our membership family. Our members and strategic partner
contentHtml:
The Women’s Council of REALTORS® San Antonio Network has had an incredible fall season filled with connection, celebration, and momentum as we continue to build relationships and grow our membership family. Our members and strategic partners have shown up in true Women’s Council fashion—collaborating, supporting one another, and making an impact in our industry and community.

On Sept. 25, our network hosted one of our most anticipated gatherings of the year—the Black and White Social & Member Appreciation Event. This gathering was held at the Edison Experiment, a venue known for its charm and intimate atmosphere. The setting couldn’t have been more perfect for an evening of networking, laughter, and celebration.

We were thrilled to welcome more than 50 attendees, including current and prospective members, strategic partners, and special guests. It was a wonderful opportunity to recognize the hard work and dedication of our network throughout the year, as well as the strong relationships that have made our organization so successful.

One of the most meaningful moments of the evening was the pinning of nine new members into our San Antonio Network. Each new member was recognized and officially welcomed into the Women’s Council family—a proud tradition that reinforces our shared commitment to leadership, collaboration, and professional growth. These new members bring fresh energy and diverse experiences to our network, and we are excited to see them thrive and contribute in the months ahead.

As always, the event was filled with fellowship, laughter, and plenty of photos. The black-and-white theme added flair to the celebration. From heartfelt conversations to fun photo opportunities, the energy in the room was undeniable.

REALTOR® Olympics – Coming Oct. 29

The excitement doesn’t stop there! Our network is gearing up for one of our favorite annual traditions—the Third Annual REALTOR® Olympics, scheduled for Oct. 29 at Raymond Russell Park. This fun-filled event combines friendly competition, team spirit, and community connection.

Teams will compete in a variety of games and challenges designed to bring out everyone’s competitive and comedic side—all while strengthening relationships among REALTORS® and strategic partners. In addition to the games, the day will feature great food, prizes, and plenty of laughter. Whether you’re participating or cheering on your colleagues, this event is sure to be one for the books.

The REALTOR® Olympics has quickly become a signature event for our network, known for its energy and ability to bring members together in a memorable way. It’s a reminder that while we work hard in this industry, we also know how to have a good time and celebrate each other’s successes along the way. This year, we’ve chosen the Winston School San Antonio as our benefiting charity. Please sign up and participate for an amazing cause.

Strategic Partner Appreciation – Nov. 5

Following the REALTOR® Olympics, we’ll turn our attention to another important celebration—our Strategic Partner Appreciation Event on Nov. 5. This gathering is dedicated to the incredible businesses and professionals who support our network throughout the year.

Our strategic partners are a vital part of what makes the Women’s Council of REALTORS® San Antonio Network thrive. Their ongoing contributions—through sponsorships, event participation, education, and collaboration—help make our programming possible. This event will give us a chance to express our gratitude and celebrate the partnerships that strengthen our mission and our members’ success.

As we move through the final months of 2025, our network continues to focus on growth, leadership development, and member engagement. With each event, we aim to create spaces where REALTORS® and industry professionals can connect, learn, and lead together.

This year has been one of momentum and meaning—welcoming new members, expanding our reach, and creating memorable experiences that remind us why the Women’s Council is such a special organization. Our theme of collaboration and appreciation has carried through every event, reinforcing our commitment to lifting each other up and building leaders for both our industry and our community.

We look forward to ending the year strong, celebrating our members and partners, and setting the stage for an even more impactful 2026.

From elegant socials to spirited competitions, one thing remains constant—the Women’s Council of REALTORS® San Antonio Network continues to grow, thrive, and lead with purpose.

head: The Biggest Mistake Agents Can Make After The Closing
excerpt: In the real estate profession, the closing table is often viewed as a finish line—a culmination of months of showings, negotiations, inspections, and financing hurdles. Yet, as many experienced brokers and coaches point out, this mindset is
contentHtml:
In the real estate profession, the closing table is often viewed as a finish line—a culmination of months of showings, negotiations, inspections, and financing hurdles. Yet, as many experienced brokers and coaches point out, this mindset is one of the most detrimental habits in the industry.

The biggest mistake real estate agents make after closing is simple but costly: they stop communicating with their clients once the deal is done. Fewer than one in ten agents maintain consistent contact with past clients beyond the first twelve months after closing. This “silent period” costs the average agent thousands of dollars in repeat and referral business annually.

Why the Mistake Happens

Closing Feels Like “Mission Accomplished”

After weeks of high-pressure transactions, closing feels like the end of a marathon. The agent’s obligations under the contract are fulfilled, and both parties are ready to move on. However, the period after closing is one of the most powerful opportunities to deepen professional relationships.

Lack of a Structured Follow-Up System

Few agents have a formalized post-closing plan. Without a clear system of reminders or a client relationship management (CRM) strategy, maintaining communication after the sale becomes sporadic or forgotten. Agents who fail to systematize their follow-up efforts miss valuable opportunities to strengthen relationships and secure future referrals.

The Pressure of the
Next Deal

In a commission-based industry, the incentive structure often rewards immediate production rather than long-term client retention. In high-demand markets such as Texas, where properties move quickly and competition is intense, many agents focus on acquiring new listings instead of nurturing past clients. As a result, repeat and referral business—often the most cost-effective source of leads—remains underdeveloped.

Misunderstanding Lifetime Value

Many real estate professionals see themselves primarily as transaction facilitators rather than lifelong advisors. Yet every client’s homeownership journey includes maintenance, renovations, refinancing, and potential resale. When agents disengage after closing, they forfeit the opportunity to serve as trusted advisors throughout that journey.

The Cost of Ignoring Clients After Closing

Lost Referrals and Repeat Business

Word of mouth remains the most powerful source of new leads in the real estate industry. Clients who receive consistent, helpful communication are far more likely to refer their agent to family and friends or to use them again in the future. Conversely, when agents disappear after closing, they remove themselves from consideration for repeat transactions.

Erosion of Brand and Reputation

A client who feels forgotten may still appreciate the sale, but they will not advocate for the agent. In contrast, agents who stay connected—through home-anniversary cards, seasonal updates, or neighborhood newsletters—remain top of mind. A strong follow-up culture enhances an agent’s reputation and reinforces credibility within the community.

Increased Post-Closing Risk

Abandoning the relationship immediately after closing can also carry risk. Unresolved issues—such as inspection discrepancies, warranty claims, or title questions—can escalate if clients feel unsupported. A brief follow-up within the first month after closing can prevent misunderstandings and demonstrate accountability, which protects both client satisfaction and the agent’s professional reputation.

Lost Position in a Changing Industry

As the real estate industry continues to evolve, maintaining client relationships is increasingly vital. Changing commission structures and rising transparency standards are reshaping how consumers choose their agents. In this environment, ongoing communication and trust-building are no longer optional—they are essential for professional survival.

Why This Issue Matters in Texas

Texas’s real estate market stands apart for its rapid population growth, strong sense of community, and heavy reliance on referrals. In a state where many homeowners move within the same metropolitan area, reputation compounds over time.

An agent who consistently maintains relationships with 100 past clients could reasonably expect 10 to 15 additional transactions or referrals per year, assuming a modest loyalty rate. Conversely, agents who disengage after closing begin each new year at zero—rebuilding their client base from scratch in an increasingly competitive environment.

The most significant mistake real estate professionals make after closing is disappearing—ending communication precisely when they should be nurturing the relationship. This oversight weakens credibility, limits referrals, and erodes long-term growth potential.

For brokers and agents—especially in Texas’s fast-paced and relationship-driven markets—sustained success depends on consistent, value-based engagement. Structured follow-up systems, genuine appreciation, and authentic communication turn one-time buyers into lifelong clients.

As the industry adapts to new market realities and evolving consumer expectations, the agents who remain visible, caring, and committed after closing will stand apart. In real estate, the transaction may end at the closing table, but the relationship should only just be beginning.

head: Celebrating Excellence and Give Back SABOR’S Season of Impact
excerpt: As the year winds down, the San Antonio Board of Realtors (SABOR) is closing 2025 with a mix of celebration, service and progress. From honoring the industry’s top professionals to supporting families in need, this season embodies the best
contentHtml:
As the year winds down, the San Antonio Board of Realtors (SABOR) is closing 2025 with a mix of celebration, service and progress. From honoring the industry’s top professionals to supporting families in need, this season embodies the best of what it means to be a Realtor — dedicated, compassionate and community-driven.

Step Into Wonderland: The 2025 SABOR Icon Awards

The highlight of the season will be the 2025 SABOR Icon Awards: A Brunch in Wonderland. Set for Dec. 3 from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the San Antonio Botanical Garden, this whimsical celebration invites members to step into a world of wonder as SABOR honors excellence in real estate. The event recognizes Realtors, affiliates and community leaders who have gone above and beyond in service, innovation and leadership.

“Don’t be late for a very important date!” Members are encouraged to save their seat for this magical morning of networking, recognition and inspiration. From Realtor of the Year to the Good Neighbor Award and more, the event celebrates icons across the industry who exemplify dedication and passion.

Honorees include top performers in categories such as Realtor Salesperson, Broker and Rookie of the Year; Manager of the Year; Lifetime Distinguished Service Award; and Realtor Social Media Influencer of the Year, among others. Additional recognition will be given for Property Management Specialist, Farm and Land Specialist, Commercial Specialist, Legislative Champion, Good Neighbor, Affiliate, Builder and Realtor Champion.

The 2025 SABOR Icon Awards: A Brunch in Wonderland promises whimsical décor, inspiring stories and a touch of magic as members come together to celebrate the professionals shaping the future of San Antonio real estate. Secure your ticket today!

Realtors Give Back: Volunteer Event at the San Antonio Food Bank

While SABOR celebrates excellence, the spirit of giving remains just as strong this season. On Nov. 20 from 8:30 a.m. to noon, Realtors will gather for the Realtors Give Back: Volunteer Event at the San Antonio Food Bank, located at 5200 Historic Old U.S. Highway 90.

This Thanksgiving season, Realtors are joining forces with the San Antonio Food Bank to help families in need by volunteering both in the warehouse and at curbside distribution. The event ensures that everyone in the community has a meal to be thankful for — reflecting the compassion and generosity that define SABOR members.

Those interested in participating can sign up online at Realtors Give Back: Volunteer Event at Food Bank.

Evolving to Meet Members’ Needs

The Realtor Academy has long been a cornerstone of professional development for SABOR members. As the industry evolves and technology reshapes the way we work, the academy is evolving too.

The team is currently revamping class offerings for 2026, with the goal of delivering education that is more meaningful, relevant and accessible than ever before. This reimagining of the course catalog goes beyond meeting continuing education requirements — it’s about equipping Realtors with the knowledge and tools they need to thrive in a competitive marketplace.

From in-depth courses on emerging market trends to hands-on sessions that build practical skills, SABOR is committed to helping members grow in ways that matter most to them. Listening to members has been central to this process. The academy team has gathered feedback, assessed industry needs and begun shaping new programming to ensure every SABOR member finds value in their educational experience.

It’s all about lifelong learning, professional excellence and pride in being part of a forward-thinking organization.

Simplified Reporting for Seller Concessions

Based on member and Board of Managers feedback, SABOR has made updates to simplify how seller concessions are reported once a listing has been marked as sold.

The process has been streamlined to one dropdown menu and one text field, with both fields required. This ensures that all necessary information is collected from the listing and that Realtors have the complete details needed for their CMAs.

The Seller Concessions Description dropdown has been simplified to include Closing Costs, Home Warranty, None and Other — see agent remarks. Multiple reporting fields have been consolidated into a single field designed to capture one dollar amount for the “Total Amount Paid by Seller.” Seller concessions in the MLS reflect the amount paid by the seller toward the buyer’s closing costs.

Strengthening the Realtor Community

As SABOR continues to build on its pillars of advocacy, education and networking, the organization’s focus remains the same — empowering members to succeed, advocating for the future of real estate and nurturing a network of professionals who support one another and their communities.

Together, we can shape the future of real estate.

head: Future of SA: Growth, Equity, and The Impact of Prop A and B
excerpt: San Antonio stands at a unique moment in its development trajectory. Rapid population growth, major economic investment and transformational downtown initiatives are converging to reshape the region’s real estate future. Two of the most inf
contentHtml:
San Antonio stands at a unique moment in its development trajectory. Rapid population growth, major economic investment and transformational downtown initiatives are converging to reshape the region’s real estate future. Two of the most influential voices in that evolution — Jeff Webster, president and CEO of the Greater San Antonio Chamber of Commerce, and City Councilwoman Sukh Kaur of District 1, and broker/owner of NAI Excel — offer perspectives that capture both the opportunities and responsibilities facing the city.

With the recent passage of Propositions A and B, the future of housing, commercial development and downtown revitalization has become a central public conversation. Webster and Kaur, though approaching the issue from different lenses, express optimism about what lies ahead while emphasizing different priorities for how San Antonio should grow.

Jeff Webster: Regional Growth, Economic Momentum and Strong Support for Propositions A and B

Jeff Webster has consistently framed San Antonio as a city on a solid upward trajectory. He emphasizes that the region’s current growth patterns are not temporary, stating confidently:

“San Antonio will continue to grow. We are at a growth rate of 3-4% every year. This will continue. Decreased rates will help. Residential and commercial real estate will continue to grow.”

For Webster, population growth, favorable lending conditions and industrial expansion all point toward a sustained increase in both housing demand and commercial development. He often highlights areas such as the Southeast Side as emerging “boom zones,” where large tracts of land and infrastructure capacity make new subdivisions and job centers likely.

Webster’s broader economic outlook is grounded in the idea that San Antonio’s affordability — relative to Austin, Dallas or other major metros — makes it uniquely positioned for continued expansion. Manufacturing, logistics, automotive production and corporate investment are reinforcing long-term job creation, which he views as the backbone of a healthy real estate market.

Webster on Propositions A and B

Webster was one of the civic leaders urging voters to support Propositions A and B, seeing them as catalysts for major regional benefits. After the propositions passed, he summed up their significance:

“Passage of Propositions A and B will enable continued investment to our way of life. It will bring synergy and energy for downtown. There is no downside.”

He points to the rodeo and its future growth:

“Rodeo will continue expanding on the Eastside, from 375K to 700K visitors,” and reaffirmed that event programming will stay robust: “Rodeo and other related events will continue at Frost Center.”

For Webster, these investments will create a multiplier effect, accelerating downtown revitalization, boosting tourism, generating new mixed-use projects and increasing demand for housing across the region.

Webster on the San Antonio–Austin Regional Future

Webster also acknowledges the growing conversation around the San Antonio-Austin corridor, but rejects the idea that it will become a singular metroplex:

“San Antonio and Austin will become a region, not a metroplex. Fort Worth and Dallas are much closer in distance than our two cities. We will still have distinct needs and interests. How do we connect infrastructure and roadways will be the next concern.”

His view aligns with a regional model where the two cities share economic momentum yet maintain unique identities, zoning philosophies and community priorities — something he argues will influence transportation, housing and commercial real estate planning for decades.

Sukh Kaur: Downtown Revitalization, Housing Equity and Guided Growth

City Councilwoman Sukh Kaur views real estate through a central-city lens, emphasizing the importance of affordability, inclusivity and preventing displacement as downtown undergoes rapid change.

With rising demand and major planned developments, Kaur warns that San Antonio must avoid the crises seen in other high-growth Texas metros:

“There is a lot of work we have to do in terms of housing, especially in housing. We don’t want to have prices skyrocket like in Austin. Revitalizing areas downtown.”

Kaur has been a vocal supporter of integrating affordable housing in walkable downtown areas, pushing for developments on key parcels near Hemisfair and the urban core. She believes affordability should not be pushed outward but embedded into the city’s cultural and economic heart.

Her work with the San Antonio Housing Trust Foundation — such as supporting the purchase and preservation of the low-income Robert E. Lee Apartments — reflects her commitment to ensuring growth does not come at the cost of displacement.

Kaur on Propositions A and B

Kaur supported the passage of Propositions A and B but emphasized that new investment must be paired with community benefit:

“Propositions A and B create more momentum in downtown. Developers see the city is creating growth.”

She also highlighted the unprecedented scale of the $75 million community reinvestment commitment tied to the initiative: “$75 million community reinvestment. This is more than Washington Commanders are spending on the entire city.”

For Kaur, the propositions’ success signals that residents want revitalization, but she stresses that it must be done responsibly — expanding housing options, ensuring affordability and keeping longtime residents in the communities they built.

Where Their Visions Meet

Although Webster and Kaur focus on different sides of San Antonio’s growth — regional economics versus urban-core equity — their perspectives converge on several key principles:

1. San Antonio is growing rapidly and will continue to do so.

   Both acknowledge population expansion as a defining force shaping real estate.

2. Housing supply must increase in multiple forms.

   Webster focuses on suburban and regional growth; Kaur on urban infill and affordable housing.

3. Propositions A and B will reshape downtown both economically and socially.

   Webster sees economic synergy.

   Kaur sees revitalization — but insists on equity and affordability.

4. The region must prepare for long-term infrastructure and connectivity challenges.

   Webster’s remarks about the Austin-San Antonio region connect directly to Kaur’s focus on dense, walkable housing tied to transportation.

A Combined Vision for the Future

Together, Webster and Kaur offer a powerful dual framework for the future of San Antonio real estate:

• Strong economic growth with continued job creation

• More housing — both suburban and urban — across all income levels

• Major downtown reinvestment, strengthened by Propositions A and B

• A commitment to affordability, avoiding Austin-style displacement

• Long-term regional planning between San Antonio and Austin

• A real estate market that expands outward while revitalizing inward

San Antonio stands on the brink of becoming one of the nation’s most balanced, opportunity-rich and culturally grounded growth stories. With Webster’s emphasis on economic momentum and regional development, and Kaur’s insistence on equitable, inclusive revitalization, the city has a pathway to evolve without losing its identity — and to build a future that benefits residents across every neighborhood and income level.

We recently held our 2026 Governing Board installation on Dec. 9, themed Golden Era Glamour, and I was proudly pinned by my daughters, Katherine and Elizabeth. It was an amazing evening filled with inspiration and fun.

My journey with the Women’s Council began four years ago — simply as a favor to a friend. That small favor opened a meaningful chapter of my life that grew into a passion, and that passion evolved into purpose. I have come to live this mission and to witness firsthand the power of women uplifting women.

As we look ahead to 2026, I am filled with excitement. I am deeply committed to elevating women as business owners, as leaders and as unstoppable forces.

Because I come from a close-knit family made up almost entirely of strong women — and one very patient Papa — including our newest little star, Margaret, this work is profoundly personal to me.

To my family and my loves, your unwavering support keeps me going. You amaze me every day.

To my incredible team, thank you. I ask that we continue to show each other grace, support and straighten each other’s crowns.

Thank you so much to our sponsors, Legacy Mutual Mortgage and CELKA Construction, for their gold-level sponsorship, as well as the many companies that purchased tables. You made the night a success.

To our guests, thank you for taking time out of your lives on a Tuesday to support us.

Now, to why we held the event at the American Legion. Our very own, the late Pat Farrell, was a member here and our longest-serving Women’s Council of REALTORS® member. Her legacy continues to shine within these walls.

• struggle with visibility,

• hesitate to pursue leadership roles,

• underestimate their worth, or

• juggle personal and professional pressures silently.

The council creates space for women to step into their power, reminding them:

You are capable.

You are worthy.

You are needed.

And your leadership matters.

We look forward to welcoming you.

head: Texas REALTORS® Details Sweeping Form Changes
excerpt:
Form Changes

contentHtml:
Form Changes

Texas REALTORS® has announced extensive revisions, retirements and additions to its residential, leasing and property management forms, with most changes taking effect Jan. 1, 2026, to comply with new state laws and updated Texas Real Estate Commission requirements.

The updates reflect recent legislative action, including Senate Bill 1968, Senate Bill 17, Senate Bill 38 and eviction reform laws, as well as changes to the Texas Real Estate License Act, or TRELA. Several revisions also aim to improve clarity, consistency and usability across commonly used contracts.

Residential forms revised

Among the most significant residential changes is the removal of all references to subagency from multiple listing and amendment forms, including the Residential Real Estate Listing Agreement Exclusive Right to Sell (TXR 1101), Farm and Ranch Real Estate Listing Agreement (TXR 1201) and Amendment to Listing (TXR 1404). Subagency is being eliminated from TRELA effective Jan. 1, 2026.

The residential listing agreement also adds the T-47.1 Declaration as an option and includes broader language cleanup, including capitalization of defined terms. Similar clarity-focused revisions were made across several addenda and notices, including the Condominium Addendum to Listing (TXR 1401), which replaces the word “unit” with “property” throughout.

Texas REALTORS® is also retiring the “Buying Your Home: Settlement Costs and Helpful Information” HUD form (TXR 2512) due to lack of use.

Buyer representation updates and new forms

The Buyer/Tenant Representation Agreement – Long Form (TXR 1501) was expanded to apply beyond residential transactions by removing “Residential” from the title. The form now allows for an optional broker retainer, defines “related party,” and includes an informational notice about Senate Bill 17, which restricts certain foreign acquisitions of real property.

Termination and consumer notice forms were also revised to clarify signature requirements, termination fees, survival of provisions and protections periods.

Two new residential forms are being introduced:

Unrepresented Customer Showing Form (TXR 1508), designed for non-agency showings following changes under SB 1968.

Residential Contract Critical Date List (TXR 1958), an informational tool to help track deadlines in one-to-four family contracts.

Leasing and property management changes

Leasing and property management forms underwent broad updates to align with new laws and an extensively revised Residential Lease.

The Residential Real Estate Listing Agreement Exclusive Right to Lease (TXR 1102) now reflects new broker compensation requirements, includes Fair Credit Reporting Act notices and adds insurance provisions. References to subletting and assignment fees were removed to align with updated lease language.

Numerous lease-related addenda and notices were updated to match newly renumbered lease paragraphs, while the Residential Lease Sight Unseen Addendum (TXR 2017) was retired because its language is now included directly in the lease.

The Residential Lease (TXR 2001) and Residential Lease for a Multi-Family Property Unit (TXR 2011) received extensive restructuring. Changes include reorganized rent and fee disclosures, clearer termination and renewal provisions, revised security deposit language, updated maintenance and repair responsibilities, and new options for email delivery of notices when agreed to in writing.

A new Notice to Pay or Vacate (TXR 2232) was also created to comply with eviction reform laws taking effect Jan. 1, 2026, which in certain cases require landlords to provide this notice instead of a traditional Notice to Vacate.

TREC-mandated form updates

Several Texas Real Estate Commission forms were revised or replaced:

Information About Brokerage Services (TXR 2501, IABS 1-2) becomes mandatory Jan. 1, 2026, replacing IABS 1-1. Updates remove subagency references, explain when written agreements are required and clarify when license holders may show property without representation.

Seller’s Temporary Residential Lease (TREC 15-7) and Buyer’s Temporary Residential Lease (TREC 16-7) become mandatory Jan. 5, 2026, replacing prior versions and removing flood notice requirements for temporary and short-term leases.

Texas REALTORS® advises members to begin familiarizing themselves with the new forms and requirements ahead of the January deadlines to ensure compliance and smooth transactions under the updated legal framework.

head: New Leadership, New Year: Zapata Highlights SABOR’s Direction for 2026

contentHtml:
As we begin 2026, I am honored to serve as chair of the San Antonio Board of REALTORS® and to work alongside an accomplished and dedicated Board of Directors. Our installation earlier this month marked more than the start of a new leadership year — it reaffirmed SABOR’s long-standing commitment to professionalism, advocacy and service.

SABOR has thrived for more than a century because of leaders who understood that strong associations are built on integrity, collaboration and forward thinking. That legacy was evident during our installation ceremony, where past presidents and chairs joined us in the ceremonial passing of the gavel — a reminder that while leadership changes, our mission remains constant.

This year, the Board and Executive Committee are focused on ensuring SABOR continues to deliver meaningful value to members while positioning our association for the future. That includes supporting REALTORS® through education, protecting private-property rights through advocacy and making strategic investments that help members grow their businesses in an increasingly competitive marketplace.

One of those investments is SABOR’s ongoing consumer marketing effort.

Don’t Miss the Leads: Claim Your HAR Profile Today

As part of your SABOR member benefits, our marketing campaigns work year-round to promote the value of working with a REALTOR® and to drive consumers directly to SABOR-owned platforms.

In 2025, SABOR’s consumer campaign drove 47,627 users to the “That’s a REALTOR®” landing page, with nearly 100% of that traffic coming from new users. This reach was achieved through a strategic mix of paid social, paid search, display advertising and video streaming ads, demonstrating the scale and effectiveness of SABOR’s media investments.

These results show that SABOR’s campaigns successfully reached new consumers and reinforced the value of working with a REALTOR® at key moments in their decision-making journey — expanding awareness well beyond existing audiences.

What’s Changing in the New Year

In 2026, SABOR’s consumer campaigns will shift from informational landing pages to the Homes and Rentals search portal on SABOR’s websites. This change is designed to meet consumers where they are most engaged:

  • Consumers are already in an active home or rental search mindset
  • REALTOR® profiles are visible and actionable
  • Members can capture and convert leads generated by SABOR’s media spend

As part of this shift, SABOR’s marketing efforts will increase visibility for the Homes and Rentals search portal, directing motivated consumers straight to REALTOR® profiles at the moment they are ready to take action. To fully benefit from this exposure, it is essential that members claim and optimize their professional profiles.

Why Claim Your HAR Profile?

Claiming your professional profile ensures that:

  • Your contact information appears correctly with your listings
  • Consumers can easily find and connect with you directly
  • You build trust by showcasing your experience, specialties, client reviews and past transactions
  • Your profile is optimized in search results, giving you a competitive edge over unclaimed profiles

Claiming your profile is quick and easy at cms.har.com/claimprofile.

Please note: SABOR is currently working to add LERA MLS as a selectable option in the drop-down menu during the profile setup process. In the meantime, members may complete their profiles by selecting the Houston Association of REALTORS®. This selection will not impact profile visibility or functionality.

After submitting your claim, you will receive an email from HAR.com within approximately 24 to 48 hours with next steps to complete the process.

SABOR is driving the traffic. Make sure you are ready to capture the leads.

As chair, I believe our strength as an association comes from engaged members who take advantage of the resources available to them and contribute to the collective success of our industry. When REALTORS® succeed, our communities benefit.

I am grateful for the trust placed in me and for the dedication of our Board, staff and volunteers. Together, we will build on SABOR’s legacy and move forward with purpose, progress and professionalism in 2026.

head: HOLLYWOOD CRAWFORD Garage Doors and Openers
excerpt: When Randy Oliver joined his father-in-law Doyle Benton’s garage door company in 1981, he wasn’t setting out to build a decades-long legacy. He was a 21-year-old, newly married college student learning the business from the ground up. More
contentHtml:
When Randy Oliver joined his father-in-law Doyle Benton’s garage door company in 1981, he wasn’t setting out to build a decades-long legacy. He was a 21-year-old, newly married college student learning the business from the ground up. More than 40 years later, that decision has shaped not only his career but a family-owned company that has grown alongside San Antonio’s booming housing market.

Oliver’s entry into the industry was hands-on from day one at Hollywood-Crawford Garage Doors and Openers. He began installing garage doors, learning the mechanics and demands of the trade before moving into sales, management and eventually company leadership. What started as a small operation with about 20 employees has grown into a regional business with more than 70 team members serving San Antonio and surrounding communities, including New Braunfels.

The company’s roots stretch even further back. Founded after World War II by Harry Crosland, the Hollywood Crawford brand expanded across Texas through independently owned, family-run businesses. That legacy of craftsmanship and independence remains central to Oliver’s approach today.

Among the accomplishments Oliver is most proud of is his long-term service to the industry. He served 13 years on the board of the International Door Association, including two years as president, helping guide standards and build relationships across the United States and Canada. Locally, he has remained active with the Greater San Antonio Builders Association and the Greater New Braunfels Home Builders Association, partnering closely with builders as the region continues to grow.

Within the company, one of the most meaningful milestones is succession. Today, Oliver’s two sons, Chris and Jonathan, hold key leadership roles. Chris oversees daily operations, while Jonathan manages sales, ensuring the business remains family-owned while preparing for the future.

Like the real estate industry itself, Oliver’s career has weathered multiple cycles. The late 1980s were particularly challenging, with housing starts in San Antonio dropping to historic lows. Rather than retreat, the company diversified its services to keep employees working and weather the downturn.

During the 2008-09 housing crisis, a strategic partnership with a national manufacturer helped the company grow market share even as others contracted. The experience reinforced a lesson Oliver still carries: adaptability, relationships and long-term thinking matter more than short-term trends.

At Hollywood-Crawford Garage Doors and Openers, community involvement is a core value. Over the years, Oliver and his team have supported numerous local and regional organizations, including Daily Bread Ministries, One Hope for Kids, South Texas Alliance for Orphans and the S.H.A.R.E. Center, a crisis pregnancy resource in the Spring Branch area.

The company also encourages hands-on service. Leadership and sales teams have volunteered with local nonprofit organizations, reinforcing a culture that values contribution as much as performance.

One trend Oliver continues to highlight is the growing recognition of garage doors as a high-impact home improvement. According to Remodeling magazine’s Cost vs. Value report, garage door replacement consistently ranks among the top projects nationwide for return on investment, often outperforming more expensive renovations.

For newcomers to real estate or homebuilding, Oliver’s advice is practical: Pay attention to details that shape first impressions and functionality. A garage door can account for a significant portion of a home’s front elevation and is one of the most frequently used moving components in a house. Regular maintenance and thoughtful design choices can prevent costly breakdowns and add measurable value.

Outside of work, Oliver values time with family above all else. He enjoys traveling with his wife and family and has maintained a weekly basketball game since his teenage years. Today, he is joined by his sons, son-in-law and grandson — a routine that mirrors his professional life: consistency, relationships and staying active.

Whether working with national builders, custom home projects or homeowners preparing to sell, Oliver’s message is simple: Small details can make a big difference. From curb appeal to daily functionality, the right garage door — and the right partner — can add lasting value.

head: Red Flags Inspectors Wish REALTORS Knew
excerpt:
REALTORS Urged to Sharpen Inspection Awareness as Market Pressures Rise  



 In today’s fast-moving real estate market, where competition remains intense and transactions often proceed at a rapid pace, industry professionals are being urge
contentHtml:
REALTORS Urged to Sharpen Inspection Awareness as Market Pressures Rise

In today’s fast-moving real estate market, where competition remains intense and transactions often proceed at a rapid pace, industry professionals are being urged to take a more vigilant role in identifying property risks and navigating the inspection process. Two emerging guidance documents circulating among real estate professionals outline critical “red flags” and inspection best practices that could significantly impact both buyer confidence and transaction outcomes.

Experts say that while home inspections have long been a standard part of the buying process, the increasing complexity of homes — and the growing use of advanced inspection technologies — means agents must be more informed than ever before.

Structural Warning Signs Demand
Early Attention

Among the most pressing concerns highlighted for agents are visible structural issues that can signal deeper, costly problems. Sagging rooflines, for instance, are not merely cosmetic flaws but may indicate serious deficiencies in attic framing or overall structural integrity. Similarly, room additions — often attractive selling points — can pose risks if they were d without proper permits or if they have begun to separate from the main structure.

“Agents are often the first professionals to walk a property with a client,” said one industry observer. “Recognizing these early warning signs can prevent deals from collapsing later.”

Foundation issues remain another critical area of concern. Cracks wider than 1/16 inch, especially those that extend into the home’s interior, may suggest ongoing movement that could require expensive repairs. Drywall cracks, particularly those that run diagonally or horizontally rather than along joints, can reinforce suspicions of structural instability.

Roof condition is also a major factor. Missing shingles, while sometimes overlooked, may indicate that the roof system is deteriorating and nearing the end of its lifespan. Combined with poor yard drainage — such as slopes directing water toward the home — these issues can accelerate structural damage over time.

Hidden Problems Beneath the Surface

Not all red flags are immediately visible. REALTORS are encouraged to examine utility indicators and environmental conditions that may reveal hidden problems. A running water meter, for example, can signal an underground leak or a plumbing issue such as a faulty toilet. Sewer cleanouts located near large trees may point to root intrusion, particularly if standing water is observed when the cap is removed.

Environmental hazards also remain a concern, particularly in older homes. Properties built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint, posing health risks if the paint is peeling or deteriorating. Pest damage, including termite activity or rodent infestations, can often be detected through signs such as rotted siding or droppings in concealed areas like garages or under sinks.

“These are the kinds of issues that can turn a dream home into a financial burden,” one inspector noted. “REALTORS who understand them add real value to
their clients.”

Inspections: More Than a Checklist

Beyond identifying physical red flags, the documents emphasize a broader understanding of how inspections function — and what they are not.

One key point is that homes are inspected against modern building standards, even if they were constructed decades earlier. This means that many items flagged in inspection reports are not necessarily defects but rather opportunities for improvement or safety upgrades. “Buyers often see a long list of issues and assume the house is in poor condition,” said a veteran real estate agent. “But many of those items are simply recommendations to bring the home closer to today’s standards.”

Importantly, inspectors are bound by minimum standards set by regulatory bodies such as the Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC), but there is no upper limit to what they can include in a report. As a result, reports can vary significantly in length and detail, sometimes including items that are subjective or cosmetic in nature.

Preparation Is Key to a Smooth Inspection

Industry professionals stress that proper preparation can make a significant difference in how an inspection unfolds. Ensuring that all utilities are turned on and that inspectors have access to key areas — such as attics, crawl spaces, electrical panels, and water heaters — is essential.

Providing the inspector with the seller’s disclosure upfront can also help streamline the process and avoid surprises. Additionally, sellers should inform inspectors about any systems that require apps or passwords, such as smart home devices, to ensure a thorough evaluation.

The timing and context of inspections are equally important. Experts caution that an inspection represents a “snapshot in time,” reflecting only the condition of the property at the moment it is conducted. Changes in weather, usage, or maintenance can alter conditions before or after the inspection.

The Role of REALTORS During Inspections

One of the more nuanced recommendations is the active involvement of REALTORS during the inspection process. While inspectors are responsible for evaluating the property, agents play a crucial role in helping clients interpret findings and make informed decisions.

Buyers are strongly encouraged to attend inspections to gain firsthand understanding of the property’s condition. Meanwhile, REALTORS attending the inspection can provide context and answer questions that fall outside the inspector’s scope, such as market implications or negotiation strategies. “Inspectors report what they see, but they don’t advise on whether a buyer should proceed,” said a brokerage manager. “That’s where the agent’s expertise comes in.”

Technology Reshaping the Inspection Landscape

The integration of advanced technologies is also transforming how inspections are conducted. Modern inspectors increasingly use tools such as drones, thermal imaging cameras, electronic levels, and even robotics to identify issues that might otherwise go unnoticed.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to play a role as well, helping inspectors analyze data and generate more comprehensive reports. While these technologies can enhance accuracy and thoroughness, they also raise expectations among buyers and agents alike. “Technology is raising the bar,” one inspector explained. “Agents need to understand what these tools can reveal so they can better prepare their clients.”

Transparency and Privacy Considerations

Another emerging issue is the presence of surveillance devices during inspections. With the growing prevalence of smart home technology, sellers may have cameras — both visible and hidden — recording activity within the home.

Industry guidance recommends that all parties be informed of any such devices to avoid privacy concerns, particularly during discussions about the inspection findings. “This is an area where communication is critical,” said a legal expert. “Failure to disclose recording devices could lead to disputes.”

A More Informed Approach to Real Estate

Taken together, these recommendations point to a broader shift in the real estate industry: a move toward greater transparency, education, and proactive risk management.

For REALTORS, the message is clear. Understanding both the physical warning signs of property issues and the nuances of the inspection process is no longer optional — it is essential.

As the market continues to evolve, those who can effectively guide clients through these complexities are likely to stand out. Whether it’s spotting a subtle foundation crack, preparing a home for inspection, or helping a buyer interpret a detailed report, informed agents are increasingly becoming indispensable partners in the transaction process. “In the end, it’s about protecting clients and ensuring successful outcomes,” said one industry leader. “Knowledge is the most valuable tool a REALTOR can bring to the table.”

head: Navigating Change with Confidence
excerpt: The San Antonio real estate market continues to evolve, and what we are experiencing today reflects a complex transition rather than a disruption. Over the past several years, we have become accustomed to a pace that was, in many ways, unsu
contentHtml:
The San Antonio real estate market continues to evolve, and what we are experiencing today reflects a complex transition rather than a disruption. Over the past several years, we have become accustomed to a pace that was, in many ways, unsustainable. Today’s environment feels different, not because the market is weakening, but because it is normalizing.

We are seeing homes spend more time on the market, inventory levels increasing, and buyers approaching decisions with greater care. At the same time, pricing has remained relatively stable, which reinforces that demand is still present and indicates that pricing needs to be more measured and intentional.

As REALTORS, this type of market calls for a higher level of awareness and a deeper understanding of our role. In a fast-moving market, speed can sometimes mask the need for strategy. In a more balanced environment, strategy becomes essential. Buyers are no longer making quick decisions with limited information; they are evaluating options, asking better questions, and expecting clear guidance. Sellers, in turn, must be positioned more thoughtfully, with pricing, presentation, and timing all working together.

This shift does not diminish our value. Rather, it highlights the tremendous need to provide greater value and expertise. Our ability to interpret the market and translate it into meaningful advice is what creates confidence for our clients.

Confidence in this environment is not about having all the answers or predicting every outcome. It comes from preparation and consistency in how we approach our business. The fundamentals matter more than ever. Pricing a home correctly at the outset, setting realistic expectations, and maintaining consistent communication throughout the process are critical components for success. These fundamental skills have proven essential over time.

While overall sales activity has softened compared to previous years, the market is still active, and opportunities continue to exist for those who are prepared to meet the moment. What has changed is that transactions now require more thought, more care and a more deliberate approach.

This type of market also places a greater emphasis on professionalism. Clients are paying closer attention to how we guide them, how we communicate, and how we manage the complexities of a transaction. They are looking for someone who can bring clarity to uncertainty and provide a steady presence throughout the process. Professionalism is not defined by how we perform when everything is easy; it is defined by how we show up when the process requires more effort, more patience and more expertise. That includes a commitment to continued education, ethical decision-making, and a focus on delivering value at every stage of the transaction.

Equally important is the strength of our professional community. While each of us runs our own business, we are part of something larger through SABOR. The ability to share insights, exchange ideas, and learn from one another becomes increasingly valuable in a market like this. The conversations we have with our peers, whether about pricing strategies, negotiation approaches, or shifting consumer behavior, help elevate all of us. Our association exists to support that collaboration, providing the tools, education, and resources needed to navigate change with confidence.

As we move forward, it is important to remember that change is a constant in real estate. The market will continue to shift, and conditions will continue to evolve. What remains consistent is the role we play in helping our clients make informed decisions.
